abstract: Populism may not only have contemporary but also long-term effects on the macroeconomy. Using data for advanced economies and emerging markets since 1960, this column explores the historical links between populist regimes, fiscal monetisation, and inflation, and how these links affect monetary policy in the 21st century. Historically, left-leaning populist regimes are linked to increases in central bank lending to the central government. In turn, central bank lending is associated with marked increases in inflation. Today, central banks with a history of deficit monetisation and left-wing populist regimes respond more strongly to deviations of inflation expectations from target, suggesting they still need to signal their independence more forcefully.
authors: Luis I. Jácome, Nicolas Magud, Samuel Pienknagura, Martín Uribe
title: Fiscal populism and monetary policy rules

abstract: Innovation has increasingly become a team activity, while inventors have become more concentrated in large firms. This column argues that these trends are closely connected. Team production creates genuine scale advantages in innovation, but can also lead the competitive economy to concentrate inventive activity too heavily in large firms because firms do not internalise knowledge spillovers.
authors: Seula Kim, Jane Olmstead-Rumsey, Honghao Wang
title: Ideas and firm dynamics when it takes two to tango
